item.title: Upper Trapezius — Shoulder Girdle Position of Ease
clinicalUse: A patient points to a tender superior shoulder after a long laptop session. Moving the head or lowering a tense shoulder reproduces their familiar ache.
Use as a comfort-based positional trial only when shoulder/neck screening supports a local muscular contribution.
Compare a comfortable head turn and arm reach before and after; neither one has to improve automatically.
patientPosition: Supine or supported sitting, with head and upper limb fully supported so the patient does not have to hold the shoulder in the air.
A pillow under the treated arm helps the scapula elevate comfortably without the clinician forcing the neck.
therapistPosition: Stand at the head/side of the table with one hand supporting the shoulder girdle and the other guiding head position if needed.
Watch for jaw clenching or global bracing; a 'position of ease' that requires effort is missing the point.
stabilization: Support the head and arm, keeping the rest of the trunk relaxed and avoiding end-range cervical loading.
Hold the scapular/shoulder girdle position lightly rather than pushing forcefully toward the ear.
contact: Light monitoring contact over the selected upper-trapezius tender area; avoid the anterior neck and supraclavicular neurovascular structures.
Use the supporting hand to position shoulder elevation while the head moves gently toward the treated side if tolerated.
forceDirection: Shorten the target upper trapezius region through comfortable ipsilateral cervical side-bending together with scapular elevation, then fine-tune toward maximal ease.
Do not side-bend away into stretch or demand a fixed rotation direction; choose according to monitored comfort.
dosage: A trained clinician may use a comfortable 60–90-second hold according to the SCS variation, then return very slowly.
Check tolerance before repetition. Repeated holds are optional, not a reward for producing tenderness.
steps: Ask the patient to show a familiar upper-shoulder symptom during head turning or arm elevation, and record it.
Screen the neck/shoulder region for neurological, vascular and serious pathology concerns.
Support the patient supine; identify a representative tender area using gentle contact.
Elevate the ipsilateral shoulder girdle and softly side-bend the head toward the tender side to shorten the region.
Adjust only within comfort until monitoring tenderness settles, with no voluntary contraction required.
Maintain the selected ease position for the protocol hold and return slowly to supported neutral.
Recheck the original head turn or arm movement and use a suitable active movement if the trial helps.
reassess: Same active cervical side-bend or rotation
Tenderness and confidence during normal postural movement
mistakes: Moving the head away from the treated upper trapezius while claiming to shorten that region.
Letting the patient actively hold the shoulder up during a supposedly relaxed positioning technique.
Using a tender point to justify ignoring neurological symptoms or referred pain.
safety: Do not force cervical rotation, extension or shoulder elevation in an irritable neck.
Stop and assess if dizziness, unusual headache, visual symptoms, neurological symptoms or unexpected symptom spread occurs.
Avoid direct pressure in the supraclavicular fossa and respect recent shoulder/neck surgery.
item.visualCue: Upper-trapezius ease = supported shoulder elevation + head side-bend toward treated side; monitor tenderness.

story.title: The shoulder has been attending every meeting
story.scene: A student arrives with the shoulders almost touching the ears. During a comfortable head turn, the upper shoulder protests. The therapist does not immediately order the muscle to 'relax'—muscles rarely obey speeches.
story.clinicalDecision: With head and arm fully supported, the clinician softly elevates the involved shoulder and side-bends the head toward that side, fine-tuning until the tender area becomes more comfortable. Neither a stretch nor a neck crank is needed.
story.retest: After a slow return to neutral, the student turns the head and reaches up again. Any improvement is checked, then followed by gentle active control and changes to the daily work task.
story.punchline: An overworked shoulder doesn't need another assignment.
story.evidenceCaveat: Positioning to ease is a clinical hypothesis; evidence does not establish a permanent muscle reset. The goal is measured symptom and movement tolerance, not structural correction.
